headline: Crude fell a third straight session on an Iran-Oman framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that single move pulled global yields down and equities up - while the POLICY conversation turned hawkish overnight, with Boston's Collins floating tightening soon and CBA saying markets now price a Fed HIKE by December. Nvidia reports in ten hours, Warsh speaks in 48
client_frame_short:
The question this morning: "oil is falling hard, stocks are up, and I keep reading that the Fed might RAISE rates - which of those is right?" All of them, and they fit together. Iran and Oman agreed a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, so crude has fallen three sessions and sits 6.6% below Monday's settle. Cheaper oil means cheaper inflation, which pulled bond yields down. **Oil is delivering the easing the Fed will not deliver itself.**

Nothing here needs a decision from you. Two things land inside the next 48 hours and both are worth knowing about rather than acting on: the Fed's preferred inflation gauge at 8:30 this morning, and Nvidia's results after the close tonight. Chair Warsh then gives his first Jackson Hole speech Friday morning. One caution on the oil story - a tanker was struck near Hormuz overnight, so the market is trading the diplomacy, not a finished peace.
client_frame:
Start with oil, because everything else this morning is downstream of it. Reuters' Wednesday wrap opens with global stocks edging up because falling oil prices pushed bond yields lower on hopes the Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen. The named cause is specific: Iran and Oman unveiled a joint framework to restore safer navigation through the Strait following talks in Tehran on Tuesday, reported by both Reuters and MarketWatch and described by OCBC in the Dow Jones EMEA briefing. Brent is roughly $86 and WTI roughly $80, third consecutive declines and the lowest since Aug 13 and Aug 10 respectively. Computed over our own held price series rather than taken from a headline: Brent is down 6.61% from Monday's $92.17 settle in two sessions, WTI down 5.52%, and Brent's monthly change has now turned NEGATIVE at -2.56%. The entire war premium built through August has been handed back. The Strait carried a fifth of the world's traded oil before the war, so this is the highest-leverage price on the board.

The bond market did the arithmetic on Tuesday, not overnight. Reuters had the 10-year at 4.625% from 4.704% late Monday, a 7.9bp rally, with the 2-year down 6.0bp and the 30-year down 6.9bp, and MarketWatch called it the lowest long-end yields since Aug 5. Overnight has been a small give-back - the 10-year is 4.647%, up 1.3bp, and the 2-year 4.207%, up 2.0bp - so read Tuesday as the event and this morning as a hold. Yesterday's $69B 2-year auction is the quiet good news: it cleared at 4.204%, roughly 11bp through the July stop, and indirect bidders, largely foreign and real-money accounts, took 66.0% of competitive awards against 56.6% in July, taken from Treasury's own results file rather than a calendar aggregator. Demand for US front-end paper is not the problem some commentary implies.

Now the part that genuinely surprised me, because it runs the other way. The policy conversation turned HAWKISH inside the same overnight window. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said the Fed may need to tighten soon absent progress on inflation, published ahead of Jackson Hole. Commonwealth Bank of Australia's Kristina Clifton says markets are now pricing a Fed rate hike by December and that CBA itself expects three hikes by mid-2027 against roughly 1.5 priced. Our own CME cohort refreshed to Tuesday's settle and still shows ZERO probability of a cut at any meeting through January 2027, with a 37.9% chance of a September hike and 69.0% cumulative by December - though every one of those figures FELL versus yesterday's cohort, consistent with Tuesday's soft data. Consumer confidence printed 89.4, the lowest since January, with the expectations component down 5.8 points, and new home sales fell 10.5% to 607,000 with the median price at a four-year low on Reuters' read. So: weak consumer, hawkish Fed talk, falling oil. Clifton's other line is the one to keep - the buyback programme eases interest costs at the margin but does not change the rising stock of debt or the concerns about fiscal dominance and Fed independence.

Two events and one caution. Nvidia reports at approximately 4:20 PM with the call at 5:00, guided to $91.0B plus or minus 2% of revenue; the number that moves the stock is the Q3 guide, where Reuters says analysts look for about $104.2B and a guide below that is the stated selloff trigger. The set-up is unusual: the VIX closed at 15.45, VIX3M at 18.21, so the term structure is in normal contango, and Reuters reports options imply a SMALLER post-earnings move than prior Nvidia prints. The market is not paying much for a binary event on a $5 trillion company. Tuesday's after-close reports rehearsed the risk precisely - Intuit, Zoom and nCino all beat on revenue and were still punished for guidance and margin trajectory, while Semtech's record data-centre quarter was rewarded. The print is not the risk; the guide is. The caution: a new tanker was struck near Hormuz overnight with Iran vowing retaliation for the US economic offensive, per the Wall Street Journal, and Treasury's promised designation of a large foreign financial institution had NOT happened as of this morning. City Index's Fiona Cincotta put it well - we really need to see the traffic move through the Strait of Hormuz before getting comfortable that inflationary pressures are cooling considerably. For clients: the useful frame today is that the cheapest form of monetary easing available right now is a lower oil price, it arrived from diplomacy rather than from Washington, and it can be taken away by a single tanker - which is exactly why we do not build plans around any one of these headlines.

geo_headlines: THE HORMUZ FRAMEWORK IS THE WHOLE MORNING, AND IT IS WORKING THROUGH OIL RATHER THAN THROUGH EQUITIES: Reuters' Wednesday global wrap opens with global stocks edging up because falling oil prices pushed bond yields lower on hopes the vital Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen. The named cause is an Iran-Oman joint framework to restore safer navigation through the Strait after talks in Tehran on Tuesday, reported by Reuters and MarketWatch and summarised by OCBC in the Dow Jones EMEA briefing; MarketWatch separately attributes part of the move to Pakistan working to revive US-Iran peace talks. Brent prints between $86.28 and $86.75 depending on timestamp, WTI between $80.29 and $80.56, third straight declines and the lowest since Aug 13 and Aug 10. Computed over our own held series: Brent -6.61% and WTI -5.52% from Monday's settles in two sessions, with Brent's monthly change now NEGATIVE at -2.56%. The Strait carried a fifth of the world's traded oil before the war.

THE DE-ESCALATION NARRATIVE IS ONE-SIDED AND THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE IS IN THE SAME OVERNIGHT WINDOW: a new tanker was struck near Hormuz overnight with Iran vowing retaliation for the US economic offensive, per the Wall Street Journal headline carried in the Dow Jones EMEA briefing at 00:16 ET. Separately, Treasury's promised designation of a LARGE FOREIGN FINANCIAL INSTITUTION - Bessent said to expect it by the end of the week - had NOT occurred as of 7:00 AM: no country named, no Chinese bank action sourceable to any wire. That is an open, dated catalyst and must not be briefed as done. AJ Bell's Dan Coatsworth on Monday's package: US sanctions on Iran were less severe than anticipated. City Index's Fiona Cincotta on the oil tape: we really need to see the traffic move through the Strait of Hormuz to get more comfortable with the idea that inflationary pressures are cooling considerably.

THE POLICY CONVERSATION TURNED HAWKISH WHILE THE PRICE ACTION EASED, AND THAT COMBINATION IS THE UNDER-PRICED FACT OF THE MORNING: Boston Fed President Susan Collins said the Fed may need to tighten SOON absent progress on inflation, published ahead of Jackson Hole. Commonwealth Bank of Australia's Kristina Clifton says markets are now pricing a Fed rate HIKE by December, with CBA itself expecting three hikes by mid-2027 against roughly 1.5 priced. Our own CME cohort refreshed to Tuesday's settle and still shows ZERO cut probability at every meeting through January 2027 - 37.9% for a September hike, 51.6% cumulative by October, 69.0% by December, 74.0% by January - though every figure FELL versus yesterday's cohort. There is no Fed speaker at all today; the Board's calendar shows none between Aug 24 and Aug 27. Lower oil is doing the easing the Committee is not.

TUESDAY'S DATA WAS UNIFORMLY SOFT AND THE HOUSING NUMBER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS TO CLIENTS: Conference Board consumer confidence printed 89.4, down from a downwardly revised 90.2 and the LOWEST SINCE JANUARY, against a 90.2 Reuters consensus, with expectations down 5.8 points to 68.2 even as the present-situation index ROSE 6.8 points to 121.2 - a classic anxious-but-employed split. Dana Peterson of the Conference Board: consumers were more pessimistic about business conditions and the labor market over the next six months. Only 5.2% intend to buy a home within six months, down from 6.5%, which Reuters calls the largest decline in more than five years - the wire's claim. New home sales fell 10.5% to 607,000 annualised from an upwardly revised 678,000, with 9.6 months of supply and a $393,800 median price that Reuters calls the lowest in four years. FHFA house prices rose 0.3% quarterly and 2.1% annually. Richmond Fed manufacturing slipped to 4 from 5 with employment turning NEGATIVE at -2.

THE 2-YEAR AUCTION WAS THE QUIET GOOD NEWS AND IT CAME FROM TREASURY'S OWN FILE, NOT AN AGGREGATOR: yesterday's $69B 2-year (CUSIP 91282CRH6) cleared at a 4.204% high yield, roughly 11bp through the July 27 stop of 4.315%, with a 2.60 bid-to-cover against 2.66 and INDIRECT bidders - largely foreign and real-money accounts - taking $44.958B, or 66.0% of competitive awards, against 56.6% in July. Primary dealers were left with only 10.9%. Pulled from the TreasuryDirect API; note for the record that a 4.315% figure circulating on calendar aggregators is the PRIOR July auction, a classic stale-row error. Today brings $70B of 5-year at 1:00 PM plus a $72B 17-week bill and a $28B 2-year FRN reopening at 11:30. DBS's Eugene Low argues Bessent's put on long-end Treasuries should not be underestimated; CBA's Clifton counters that buybacks do not change the rising stock of debt or concerns about fiscal dominance and Fed independence.

NVIDIA ARRIVES WITH THE OPTIONS MARKET REFUSING TO CHARGE FOR IT, WHICH IS THE MOST INTERESTING RISK OBSERVATION ON THE BOARD: results at approximately 4:20 PM ET with the call at 5:00, both from NVIDIA's own IR page, for the quarter ended July 26. The company guided $91.0B plus or minus 2% with non-GAAP gross margin 75.0% and excluding any China data-centre compute revenue; street revenue figures near $92B are aggregator-sourced and are NOT printed here as consensus. Reuters says analysts look for a Q3 guide near $104.2B, +82.8% year over year, and a guide below that is the stated selloff trigger; BofA's Vivek Arya is at $107-108B. Meanwhile the VIX closed 15.45 with VIX3M at 18.21 - normal contango - and Reuters reports options imply a SMALLER post-earnings move than prior Nvidia prints. VIX FUTURES term structure was not sourceable to a primary page and is not claimed. The stock snapped a seven-session losing streak Tuesday at $213.05, +2.19%.

TUESDAY NIGHT'S EARNINGS REHEARSED EXACTLY THE RISK NVIDIA FACES TONIGHT, AND THE PATTERN IS WORTH NAMING FOR CLIENTS: four of six reporters beat on revenue and the punishment was concentrated entirely in FORWARD GUIDANCE and margin trajectory. Intuit beat with adjusted EPS $4.03 on $4.35B and fell as much as 11.45% on a soft FY27 guide it partly attributes to revised stock-comp accounting. Zoom beat, RAISED its full-year guide, and fell 5.64% on a Q3 EPS guide of $1.46-1.48 against $1.50 sought. nCino raised guidance and added a $100mn buyback but missed badly on adjusted EPS at $0.05 against roughly $0.27. Semtech, the AI-infrastructure name, posted record sales of $341.9mn and record $100mn data-centre revenue, +91%, and was rewarded. Box flipped from -0.46% at 5:44 PM to +3.16% by 6:56 AM. HEICO posted record income at $1.67 a share. The print is not the risk; the guide is.

TWO POLICY FRONTS OPENED THAT ARE NOT VISIBLY PRICED, AND ONE PRIVATE-CREDIT DATAPOINT IS WORTH FILING: Canada formally retaliated Tuesday with counter-tariffs on roughly $20B (C$27.6bn) of annual US imports effective SEPT 8, at 15%, 25% and 50% across about 700 products - 50% on steel, aluminium, furniture and clothing, 25% on cheese, appliances and some seafood, 15% on electronics and tools - matching Washington dollar for dollar, plus a C$7.5B support package with interest-free BDC loans carrying no repayment for 36 months (Reuters). Reuters scales the list at nearly 4.5% of Canada's imports from the US; a WSJ framing of roughly 7% of total US imports uses a different denominator and is flagged rather than blended. Barron's read the tape as Wall Street not being sure about the Canada breakdown. Separately, an Australian private-credit fund LIMITED REDEMPTIONS overnight alongside hotter-than-expected July inflation (ABC) - small, but a real liquidity datapoint for allocators. F&M Trust CIO Warren Hurt: there are a lot of moving pieces all moving at the same time, and that is the challenge in teasing out how much each one is impacting the market.
